title.raw: Helping AI assistants find the right music tool
title.rendered: Helping AI assistants find the right music tool

content.raw:
I’m working towards making DanceFlow easier for AI assistants to find and use. Getting a plugin listed is one part of that. Helping someone reach a useful result is another, and they need different evidence.

vidIQ gives me a useful comparison. Its OpenAI listing describes recognisable jobs: researching video ideas, comparing channels and improving titles. Its MCP guide provides connection routes for several assistants, while its skills catalogue groups tools into guided workflows.

That shows how the product is presented and distributed. It doesn’t reveal why a particular assistant recommended it. OpenAI says enhanced distribution may reflect real-world usefulness and user satisfaction, and that developers cannot request that placement.

Make the small promises accurate

Looking at DanceFlow’s own package turned up changes I could make straight away. The two marketplace entries advertised version 0.1.15 while the plugin identified itself as 0.1.17. One MCP launcher still pinned 0.1.12. The OpenAI short descriptions were also longer than the current final-submission limit.

The 0.1.18 candidate brings those versions together, uses the same short description across the OpenAI manifests and adds checks to catch future drift. It replaces generic starter prompts with concrete tasks involving song analysis, lyric-video rendering and web effects that follow an audio player.

Those changes make the package clearer and remove known inconsistencies. They don’t establish that recommendation rates have improved. That needs an actual comparison.

Start with the person’s task

A large catalogue can still leave someone wondering what to do next. I’ve tightened DanceFlow’s setup guidance so it starts with the requested result, checks the relevant operation and reports the smallest missing prerequisite.

That matters because seeing a tool in a catalogue doesn’t prove its engine is ready. Some components need a separate runtime. Potbot and Unity are source previews with native-host requirements. Browser and WordPress work have their own supported routes. Setup should explain those facts before asking for more access or processing.

vidIQ’s different distribution surfaces are another reminder to check what is actually present. Its repository, installed package and public guides use different versions or workflow counts. Those namespaces and connection routes cannot be treated as interchangeable. The useful question is which operations the particular host exposes and whether they complete the intended task.

Test discovery without feeding it the answer

The next stage is a small, repeatable selection study. I’ve prepared forty task prompts: thirty routing hypotheses spanning all seventeen DanceFlow components, plus ten requests that should be handled without DanceFlow. They are proposed test cases; no agent-selection result is claimed yet.

I want to keep several questions separate. Can an assistant find the integration before it is installed? Does it suggest an appropriate installation? Can the user finish setup and complete a first task? Once enabled, does the assistant choose the right capability and avoid unnecessary calls?

Keyword awareness belongs in that work too. Ordinary phrases such as lyric timing and music analysis help explain what the tools do. Their appearance in a manifest is wording evidence, rather than a measurement of search demand. Any demand figures need a dated source and the right scope.

The sourced comparison and research questions are retained alongside the approval plan. Potbot’s discovery strategy keeps task fit, permissions and observed quality separate from ownership. The remaining work is to test these choices on real supported hosts, learn where setup fails and improve the useful result. Directory approval remains outstanding.

title.raw: Bringing Potbot and Unity into DanceFlow
title.rendered: Bringing Potbot and Unity into DanceFlow

content.raw:
DanceFlow now has two more tools in its shared catalogue: Potbot and DanceFlow for Unity. They take it in different directions. Potbot keeps coding tasks, evidence and jobs together. The Unity package brings musical clocks, shader timing and recorded movement into a game engine.

Adding their names to a list was only part of the job. The useful question was what someone could actually find, install and run, and which connections still needed work.

Keeping the joins visible

The DanceFlow toolkit now describes seventeen components through its catalogue, portable skills and packaged references. A small discovery example reads the Potbot and Unity entries without starting either host. It reports their requirements and makes the limits visible.

Potbot is still a development version. It already has durable task and evidence services, model-job records and its own database and worker routes. Preview MCP transport code exists, but a qualified Potbot-to-DanceFlow tool call still needs its own check. Finding Potbot in the catalogue does not establish that connection.

Unity has its own set of boundaries. StemLab can supply timing evidence, while DanceRudiments owns native movement and finite recordings. The Unity package consumes those contracts with explicit clocks, channel mappings and rig profiles. A recording needs to retain its source and bounds as it moves between tools.

A package version is another useful clue

The audit also found differences between release tags and package registries. On 23 October 2026, DanceRudiments had version 0.4.7 on GitHub and npm, while PyPI’s latest was 0.4.5. MediaSlide’s GitHub tag was 1.1.26, while npm served 1.0.24. Those differences matter when an installation command promises a particular feature.

The updated references keep those states separate. They link to exact source versions, current README sections, package files and examples. The release checker also distinguishes a successful check that finds no stable release from a query that failed.

The initial checks covered 189 toolkit tests and 119 WorkflowMoves tests. Unity’s standalone harnesses passed 536 managed assertions and 23 Python contract tests. Importing the complete package into Unity itself then found problems that those portable checks had not exposed.

Trying it in Unity itself

A clean project exposed a missing Particle System dependency. The native run also found a batch-test wait that did not work in that mode, plus generated rig assets and references that did not survive saving and reopening the scene.

The fixes are in Unity package 0.5.0-preview.2. On the tested Unity 6000.6.7f1, URP 17.6 and RTX 4060 Ti setup, 23 Editor cases and five PlayMode cases passed. The two synthetic skinned rigs also passed actual deformation, seeking and return-to-rest checks when their finite recordings ended. The native acceptance record keeps the host and limits explicit.

Potbot’s native check reached its configured workspace through a restricted database role. Two small model-backed task checks also passed independent readback through its local-generation route. That qualifies a specific local route; broader workloads and the DanceFlow MCP connection still need their own evidence.

Watching the deployed player move

The deployed Unity WebGL player now has a fresh hardware-renderer check. The recording below shows Arcadians playing, pausing and resuming while its clock and scene change. It was captured on the RTX renderer and is deliberately silent.

What the silent clip shows: the player starts in Ready. Play advances the Arcadians counter and changes the landscape and helix. Pause holds the song counter, then Resume continues it. The original controls stay visible.

The browser still reports some CoreCopy and HDR debug shader warnings. This establishes the observed playback path on that host. Other graphics paths, licensed real-character retargeting, exact song alignment and physical timing still need separate checks.

The shared WorkflowMoves guidance now carries these distinctions into the relevant workflows. The aim is to make the next useful step easier to find, while leaving enough evidence to see what has actually been done.

title.raw: Looking inside Arcadians, one stem at a time
title.rendered: Looking inside Arcadians, one stem at a time

content.raw:
The Arcadians example now joins together several parts of StemLab that were previously easier to inspect separately. A complete run takes the unchanged song master, separates six audio stems, estimates MIDI notes for the five pitched stems, and places all of that alongside the lyrics, section cues and tempo evidence on one timeline.

There are separate audio tracks for vocals, drums, bass, guitar, piano and other. Basic Pitch estimated 3,677 notes across bass, guitar, piano, vocals and the catch-all “other” stem. The drums remain available as audio; this recipe doesn’t pretend that it has produced a drum score.

The notes are a model’s interpretation, rather than the original MIDI behind the recording. They still need musical judgement. The same distinction matters for tempo: the confirmed 145 BPM reference stays separate from the detected beat evidence, so changing a display grid never changes the recording.

The original files stay intact. StemLab writes new analysis and MIDI files beside the source material, while StemMoves imports copied assets into a separate editing project. The current project contains 48 timed lyric lines, ten canonical section cues and the same 145 BPM reference. Cutting, splicing or rendering creates another file rather than replacing the source.

The complete recipe now lives in StemLab’s existing Arcadians workflows. Continuous integration checks the source hashes and native MIDI files, builds the viewer, tests playback and painted note lanes, and only then deploys the result. The lyrics and audio selector follow the same source clock, which means a separated stem can be auditioned against the same timing evidence as the master.

Open the complete Arcadians timeline. The source and checks are also available in the StemLab repository, the complete analysis run and the analysis guide.

This builds on my earlier introduction to StemLab, which already covered its MIDI analysis. The new part is the repeatable full-song workflow: real separated audio, native MIDI downloads, timing evidence and an original-preserving editor hand-off in one tested route.

title.raw: California Screamin’: finding warmth in a storm
title.rendered: California Screamin’: finding warmth in a storm

content.raw:
The artwork for California Screamin’ puts the Golden Gate Bridge under a huge, dark sky. The people are small against the cables and towers, but they are moving together. A warm break in the clouds stops the rain from feeling bleak.

That contrast comes from the song. Its lyrics move from traffic, wind and sudden rain into laughter and release. The last line leaves the crossing unfinished: “Never made the other side / Still felt like we arrived.” The image needs to keep that sense of a moment happening, without showing an ending the song doesn't give us.

The first three-panel carousel uses the existing cover. One panel keeps the complete artwork and title; another brings the figures and bridge closer; the final panel returns to the full release image and planned date. Keeping the same artwork across the sequence makes the change in scale do the storytelling.

There are also three separate photographic studies: a stormy overlook, a rain-soaked walkway and a close view of the bridge cables. They test how far the visual world can move beyond the cover while keeping its bridge orange, wet reflections and amber light. They are AI-generated concepts, not documentary photographs. The walkway study has three anonymous figures, so it would need its own context rather than standing in for the four people on the cover.

California Screamin’ is planned for 15 January 2027. The release page holds the current song story and artwork.

title.raw: Testing private downloads across two WordPress server setups
title.rendered: Testing private downloads across two WordPress server setups

content.raw:
Featured artwork: a generated illustration of the article’s subject. Screenshots and demonstrations below show the actual work.

DanceVault is the WordPress component I've been building for encrypted, password-controlled file delivery. It keeps private uploads out of the public Media Library and provides explicit expiry and revocation.

The useful milestone in the 1.0 series is its hosting acceptance work. The exact 1.0.1 release ZIP was exercised behind Apache and nginx, using two WordPress/PHP combinations and real TLS. The release records 142 passing checks in each of those four combinations.

The tests include encrypted storage, download handling, malformed requests and packaging. The newer release also preserves private, no-store error responses on the older WordPress compatibility target. The matrix is a compatibility test record, rather than a recommendation to deploy an old PHP version.

A file is stored as authenticated ciphertext, while download handling verifies its stored size and hash before emitting plaintext. The password is kept out of the URL. Expiry and revocation prevent new requests; they cannot recall a copy someone has already downloaded.

Those results still leave the actual destination host to check. Its temporary storage, server rules, HTTPS configuration and limits matter before private files are used. This release record does not establish a production installation or an independent security audit.

The release and exact assets link to the hosting acceptance guide. That makes the milestone reproducible while keeping its practical limits visible.

title.raw: Making a keyword shortlist that keeps its reasons
title.rendered: Making a keyword shortlist that keeps its reasons

content.raw:
Featured artwork: a generated illustration of the article’s subject. Screenshots and demonstrations below show the actual work.

The ten-query comparison left a practical question: once there is a pool of phrases, how do I choose a small set without losing why each one was kept?

KeywordMoves 0.5.8 adds an explicit shortlist-review step. A dated review supplies the song and platform, the exact saved-pool hash, a fit judgment, an intent group and a reason for each decision. The selector applies that review while retaining the original source evidence.

I reran the released synthetic example for this article. It selected five phrases from six supplied candidates and excluded friendship songs for preschool because the supplied review marked that fit ineligible. The run made no network requests and supplied no real search-volume estimates. The figure is a rendered summary of that actual output.

By default, the selector keeps up to five direct, naturally worded listening targets, with at most two from each declared intent group. A shortage remains a shortage. Grouping comes from the supplied review; the tool does not independently discover the best semantic clusters or decide what a song means.

The hash check also matters. If the candidate pool changes, an old review cannot quietly be applied to different evidence. Original provider scores, dates, geography and units remain distinct from editorial priority, and selection alone does not adopt a campaign keyword.

This is a decision record after research, rather than another demand model. The review contract and executable example show the inputs, rejection reasons and safeguards.

title.raw: Arcadians is video-indexed. That isn’t the same as being found.
title.rendered: Arcadians is video-indexed. That isn’t the same as being found.

content.raw:
On 13 October I published a small watch-page experiment for Arcadians.

The question was deliberately narrow. The main release page already had the song, artwork, lyrics and video, but Google’s video report said the video was not on a watch page. I wanted to see whether a separate page, built around actually watching that one video, would let the search engine understand it properly.

Two days later, the technical part worked. Google had indexed the page, detected the correct YouTube video for Arcadians, classified the page as a watch page and marked the video as indexed.

That sounds like success, but it is only one kind of success.

The performance check tells a more useful story. In the settled 28-day window ending 26 October, the main Arcadians page had 36 web-search impressions, up from 6 in the previous equal window, but no clicks. Its average position moved from 5.33 to 10.39. The watch page itself had no qualifying rows in the exact-page Web, Video or Search appearance tables.

Those facts do not prove that the watch page caused anything. They also do not establish a real zero-traffic baseline: “No data” is not the same thing as a measured zero, and the earlier comparison window predates the page entirely. The complete post-publication 28-day window will not end until 10 November, and Search Console still needs time to settle it after that.

So I’m keeping the experiment narrow. The indexing gate passed; the audience-performance gate has not. I am not copying the same structure across every release page on the strength of technical eligibility alone.

That distinction is the interesting bit for me. A well-structured page can make a video eligible to appear. It cannot manufacture search demand, a useful query match or a click. Those need their own evidence.

The next review will keep the main release page and the watch page separate, look for actual Video-search or video-appearance rows, and compare complete settled windows rather than celebrating a green indexing label. Until then, Arcadians has a correctly indexed video page — and a test that is doing exactly what a useful test should do: stopping me from claiming more than the evidence says.

title.rendered: MediaSlide: one collection, four ways to browse

content.raw:
Featured artwork: a generated illustration of the article’s subject. Screenshots and demonstrations below show the actual work.

Sometimes a collection is easiest to scan as a list. Sometimes the useful part is its metadata, a contact sheet or one large image. MediaSlide brings those four views into a responsive React media browser.

content.raw:
Featured artwork: a generated illustration of the article’s subject. Screenshots and demonstrations below show the actual work.

PrismMoves gives me a more structured way to examine an image before extending its visual language. It calls PixelCue for the measurements and organises the result into an evidence ledger, a readable report and a self-contained HTML view.

For this article, I ran the newly generated illustration through the current PrismMoves 0.2.0 and PixelCue 0.9.1 runtime. The report below is actual output from that run. The illustration is conceptual artwork; the palette and spatial measurements are computed from its pixels.

The source is 1536 by 1024 pixels, analysed at 768 by 512. Its sampled palette includes a warm pale neutral at about 23 per cent and a blue centre at about 10 per cent. Those are approximate sampled colour centres. They give a more useful starting description than an unexplained overall quality score.

The same report records luminance, saturation, edges, texture, symmetry and spatial-frequency evidence, alongside the image hash and colour handling. This run requested no semantic or OCR models. It makes no model-derived claim about the objects, emotional tone or intended meaning of the picture.

Optional captioning and embedding models can add hypotheses when they serve a real question. Their results remain separate from measurements, and unavailable analysis stays visible. A still-image report also leaves motion, responsive layout, rights and audience response to other evidence.

PrismMoves is a small reporting layer around PixelCue, rather than another image-analysis engine. The source and usage guide explain how to reproduce an individual profile and what must be reviewed before drawing conclusions about a whole collection.

title.raw: Five ways to make fire, with different trade-offs
title.rendered: Five ways to make fire, with different trade-offs

content.raw:
Featured artwork: a generated illustration of the article’s subject. Screenshots and demonstrations below show the actual work.

An animated flame can come from a recording, a group of moving image fragments or a simulation. Those choices produce different movement and need different kinds of preparation. I've brought five selectable fire methods into FrameRudiments so the choice can be made deliberately.

The comparison uses synthetic cards and a test tone. Its six panels show filmed flame, animated sprites, a 2D buoyant fluid model, procedural 3D volume rays, an actual Blender Mantaflow bake and fractured ice. During the second part, the fire methods burn away a card while the ice method freezes it.

The filmed route retains photographed flame detail. The sprite route rearranges frames through the existing particle system. The 2D solver models a bounded visual flow of fuel and heat. The volume renderer integrates a procedural density field. Mantaflow uses a real baked gas simulation. Those descriptions remain separate: a procedural volume does not become a fluid simulation simply because it looks convincing.

The shared interface provides artwork burn and freeze operations with explicit progress. At zero burn, the original artwork is retained; a completed burn is transparent. Freeze preserves the source alpha. This makes it possible to use an effect during an exit without forcing the held words through the same treatment.

The method guide covers the settings and bounds. The final choice still needs visual review for repeated shapes, bright cores, transparent edges and interference with text.

title.raw: Getting a song ready for the search spike
title.rendered: Getting a song ready for the search spike

content.raw:
Featured artwork: a generated illustration created for this article. The figures below show the measured research.

I wanted to know how much useful timing there was in releasing a Budget song on Budget day. Gilt Trip is about borrowing, spending and passing the bill along. The date gives it a reason to turn up in a conversation, but I still need to know when that conversation is happening and what people are looking for.

I started with the two previous UK Autumn Budgets. They happened on different dates: 30 October 2024 and 26 November 2025. I lined up the search data around each statement day and compared the same fourteen days before and after it.

In both GB Web Search samples, “autumn budget” reached its highest point on Budget day. The following three daily indices fell to 31, 10 and 3 in 2024, and 22, 7 and 2 in 2025. Each panel has its own scale. A hundred marks the high point of that particular request; it gives me a timing clue without telling me how many searches took place. Google's data explanation covers the sampling and low-volume limits.

The phrase “budget song” looked interesting in the 2025 music comparison. Its related searches included “best budget projectors”. That changes the meaning of the opportunity rather considerably. I kept the useful event wording and qualified it with UK Autumn Budget satire song, which tells someone what I am actually offering.

Christmas produced another useful lesson. I first compared Christmas music and several festive occasions alongside Black Friday. Black Friday reached a hundred, while Christmas music reached only two or three. Much of the smaller activity appeared as zero or less than one. Those are different source states, and neither supplies a count of people who might listen to a song.

I collected the smaller terms separately using the same dates, country and search property. The standalone Christmas-music exports contained positive values on 97–99 of the 99 days in each season. They supplied a much clearer shape. Multiplying the original twos and threes would only have enlarged the rounding.

I also collected curves from Google Trends' separate YouTube Search property. I kept those apart from the Web results. Hashtag pages supply another kind of evidence again. Their visible videos can help me inspect the company a tag keeps; their counts cannot supply a listening forecast.

The reusable workflow now starts with the actual song and listener, checks each event date, saves comparable completed cycles, and records the method before choosing a publication window. KeywordMoves 0.6.2 adds an event-cycle planner which keeps source quality and musical fit separate. It can withhold a timing recommendation when a phrase is sparse or ambiguous. Where enough years are usable, it checks a later cycle using only the earlier ones. Testing in time order matters because a graph I have already seen makes a very accommodating prediction target.

I ran nine Christmas analyses from the first set of sources, followed by three more after checking the smaller terms separately. The clearest useful results came from the occasions around the songs. Secret Santa's historical peak mapped to 4–8 December, with a broader high-interest interval of 2–11 December. Christmas dinner mapped to 24–25 December, with the peak on Christmas Day. Christmas morning and the separate YouTube Search Christmas-music series also peaked on the day itself.

That last result matters. For Web Search Christmas music, the 2025 peak arrived two days earlier than the window formed from 2023 and 2024. I have kept that miss rather than calling the wider, hindsight-informed range a successful prediction. The other rows' one successful test each are still only one test, not a reliable success percentage.

Some of the more specific song phrases had too little data to use. A standalone “sad Christmas song” request in one season reached a hundred but contained only one positive daily point. “Alternative Christmas songs” did the same in another year. The remaining standalone years lacked enough data. Those points cannot establish a recurring listening window, and there was no usable timing forecast for the individual song phrases in this study.

For Christmas Tat, the practical choice was to move an existing Secret Santa Short from 29 November to 2 December at 18:10 GMT. That puts it inside the broader Secret Santa interval, ahead of the 4–8 December peak, while avoiding a neighbouring campaign slot. The Black Friday-specific clips stay around Black Friday. Secret Santa searches include gifts and shopping, so the copy still needs to say clearly that this is a comedy song. The date is a reasoned test; the hour is an editorial choice.

For Gilt Trip, I have scheduled the existing full video for 11:30 GMT on 28 October, ahead of the Budget statement expected after Prime Minister's Questions. Parliament's notice gives approximately 12:30 for the statement. The one-hour lead is my scheduling choice. Daily curves and the lack of a usable channel audience-hours report cannot prove an optimal minute.

The saves needed one more check. Studio was displaying its current GMT+1 offset for dates after the clocks change. I checked the intended UTC instants through the native controls, then reopened the saved videos independently. The accepted schedules correspond to 11:30 in London for Gilt Trip and 18:10 for the Christmas Tat Short. They remain future schedules; the public releases and viewing results are still to come.

That leaves me with a useful plan to test: clear wording, a relevant moment and an honest account of what the evidence supports. The next comparison is with actual discovery and viewing results at comparable ages. I will keep the awkward results too.

Research sources were captured on 24 October 2026. The figures show sampled relative interest and source-resolution experiments. They do not establish absolute searches, demand for a particular original song, a hashtag effect or an increase in reach.

title.raw: Keeping the pieces of a Potbot upload
title.rendered: Keeping the pieces of a Potbot upload

content.raw:
Potbot can now keep the pieces of an unfinished upload and report which ones are missing. A client can continue from that saved state, send the remaining pieces in a different order and check the completed file against its original SHA-256 hash.

This is the other direction of the bounded artifact reads. Reading an existing output was already covered. The new work retains incoming chunks and gives each upload a durable completion record.

Five SYN Cogs handle opening an upload, storing a chunk, inspecting missing slots, committing the complete file and aborting unfinished access. They use the existing artifact store and work ledger. The authenticated workspace, owner, policy, expected length and whole-file hash stay pinned throughout.

The end-to-end test uses 131,117 synthetic binary bytes. Each chunk is at most 8 KiB, keeping the encoded request below the existing 16 KiB inline limit. After the first two chunks, fresh controller and service instances inspect the missing slots. The remaining chunks arrive backwards, followed by a repeat of the first chunk.

There are 17 unique chunks at the end. An identical repeat counts once. A repeat with different bytes is rejected. The commit assembles the ordered source through a temporary file, verifies the complete length and SHA-256, and checks current permission and expiry again before publication. The test then reads the completed artifact through the existing range Cogs and reconstructs the exact original bytes.

Two clients also try to commit the same upload concurrently. Both receive the same artifact identity. Transaction advisory locks serialize those decisions while preserving the immutable tables’ existing permissions. Inspection returns at most 128 missing offsets per page, so a large upload cannot turn into one unbounded status response.

The rejection tests cover incomplete uploads, conflicting parameters, changed policy or workspace, expired sessions, missing or corrupted staged bytes and a wrong whole-file hash. They withdraw a host grant during staging and assembly. An injected monotonic clock shift also checks the deadline guard; that is a controlled test, rather than a measured long wait.

The existing cautious write policy remains in place. A write that raises after dispatch is marked indeterminate and fences that controller. A trusted replacement must inspect the durable state under current permission before continuing. Start, actual progress and terminal statistics remain visible through the same REST and WebSocket monitoring routes.

Aborting stops further upload work. It leaves staged artifacts in place and cannot delete a committed file. Physical retention and garbage collection still need their own implementation. Chunk sizes are logical bounds; peak process memory and physical disk traffic remain unavailable where they have not been measured.

The 0.5.0.dev8 source preview and upload Cog guide retain the code and limits. This qualifies the existing local POSIX backend and controller recreation within one Python test process. Actual network disconnections, process crashes, other backends and real devices remain separate work.

title.raw: A signed trail for Potbot’s tool work
title.rendered: A signed trail for Potbot’s tool work

content.raw:
I’m giving Potbot a signed trail of its tool work. Each run records the input it received, its source and policy revisions, the child work it started and the result it retained. That gives me something concrete to inspect when a workflow stops halfway through.

This follows the checked tool contracts. Those define what can pass between operations. This step follows a particular operation and its history.

The new core uses SYN Cogs for seventeen kinds of work, with separate Cogs to seal and inspect a receipt. Every admitted operation has a distinct run identity and records its start, actual progress and completion in Potbot’s existing work ledger. Child runs point to their direct cause. Private input and output files are checked against the hashes attached to the record.

The test creates 18 linked runs. A Python command and an MCP tool really execute in separate subprocesses. Agent, model, browser and other work kinds use scripted host handlers in this fixture, so their registration is exercised without implying a live provider or device connection.

A signing step binds the complete retained trace to a small immutable manifest. Later inspection checks its signature, original input and policy, then returns bounded pages of recorded events. The test’s counter for the original handlers stayed at 16 before and after that inspection: reading the history did not repeat them. Outcome verification is kept separately and remains “not assessed”.

The fixture also compares a small Python workload with cProfile off and on. Both produce the same result hash, and the record keeps their measured durations. That is one sample with unestimated timing noise, rather than a stable performance benchmark. Target memory, GPU use and cost stay marked unavailable where no measurement exists.

Windows temporary files needed a permanent fix along the way. This Python build gives directories created with mode 0700 a protected access list. In the restricted process, that dropped the inherited access needed to use the directory. A direct comparison reproduced the failure; preserving the selected parent’s existing permissions allowed the file to be created, read and deleted.

Tests, workers, benchmarks, build scripts and native startup launchers now use a shared scratch-storage policy. It checks access before writing a payload, handles bounded transient locks and reports a retained path if cleanup is genuinely blocked. Child processes receive a usable temp root, compact names leave room for nested Windows paths, and atomic-file allocation fails immediately on an access denial. The Windows regression covers Unicode and binary files, nested output, a child process reopening a closed file and read-only-file cleanup. Native vault custody keeps its own private access rules.

The code checks changed inputs, revoked admission, foreign workspaces, incomplete traces and expired page cursors. A write with an uncertain result is recorded as indeterminate and fences further dispatch through that runtime. The recorded history remains available for reconciliation.

This is the shared core of the next implementation stage. Adopting it in every existing producer, general artifact range transport and independently testing remote hardware still have their own gates. The 0.5.0.dev6 source preview, provenance guide and Windows scratch-storage notes include the implementation and its limits.

title.raw: Giving hashtags a proper check before they go into a post
title.rendered: Giving hashtags a proper check before they go into a post

content.raw:
I've added a hashtag workbench to KeywordMoves to make the choice a little more deliberate. A plausible-looking list still leaves several questions unanswered: does each tag describe this particular clip, is it useful on this platform, and did the reviewed wording actually make it into the final caption?

The new flow keeps discovery, review and the final copy check together. It can extract literal tags from permitted saved captions, or work with clearly labelled local proposals. It keeps the source, date and platform attached. Seeing a tag in a few captions is evidence of that sample's wording; it doesn't tell us how many people search for it.

Text alternative for the silent demonstration

The discovery step contains four example tags: #ExampleSong, #IndiePop, #MusicVideo and #Viral. The review keeps the title, genre and format examples and rejects #Viral as generic reach bait. The final-copy audit confirms that the caption contains the three reviewed tags, with no extra or missing tags. The local check passes. The example's inputs and native-check assertion are synthetic; no native save, publication or improved reach is demonstrated.

Each choice needs an explicit reason and a direct connection to the content. There is no requirement to fill every available slot. The tool can hold stale research or a proposed trend that lacks recent evidence, and it keeps those reasons with the result.

The last check matters because copy can change between research and scheduling. The audit records the caption and asset hashes, and WorkflowMoves can check that receipt against the actual files in a proposed social plan. A different video, changed wording or wrong platform puts the item on hold.

Platforms also need different treatment. X recommends no more than two hashtags. Threads uses a native topic tag, while Pinterest's guidance emphasises descriptive titles, descriptions and available topics. YouTube's hashtags and video tags are separate fields. The small set sizes in this workflow are editorial starting points for testing, rather than claims about an ideal number.

The audience results will need their own evidence. A successful post doesn't establish which tag helped it, and a large lifetime post count doesn't prove that a tag is useful for this song today. The useful next step is to compare relevant choices on similar posts at the same age, keeping the other changes visible.

KeywordMoves 0.6.0 and WorkflowMoves 0.1.45 contain the new work. There's a runnable offline example and a guide to the exact inputs, checks and limits.

title.raw: Giving Potbot tools a checked contract
title.rendered: Giving Potbot tools a checked contract

content.raw:
I’ve added the next part of Potbot’s tool system: checked contracts that describe what a tool accepts, what it returns, and which installed implementation will handle the call.

A search is a small example. It receives one typed query and returns one typed result. Those values carry their exact schema identities. Another operation can check the result and round-trip it into a stable JSON representation. An unknown Type, a changed schema or a missing required field stops the call.

The new contracts cover six records: the tool description, its capability, its implementation, its workspace installation, an invocation and the resulting evidence. They build on SYN’s existing Types and property system. Required properties are inherited, defaults stay visible, and optional properties remain optional.

I’ve implemented three Cogs to exercise this: a bounded search over a host-supplied corpus, a contract validator and a unit converter. Each has one registered input Type and one registered output Type. Each records its own start, actual progress and completion through Potbot’s existing work ledger.

The unit conversion makes a useful failure visible. The fixture converts 1,250 milliseconds into 1.250 seconds while retaining the original source hash and character spans. It carries the unit, precision and allowed tolerance explicitly. Asking for a result that loses more precision than allowed produces a failure. Ambiguous dates, unknown units and an unexpected locale are rejected too.

Where rounding is permitted, the output records the amount lost. A changed schema can be checked conservatively for new optional fields, but it cannot silently replace the schema already pinned to an active call. Changed required fields or existing constraints need a new versioned contract.

A tool description still needs an installed handler and permission to run. The binding check compares its handler reference, revision, hash and exact input/output schemas with the installed Cog. The controller checks admission again immediately before dispatch. A revoked grant, a direct handler call or failed work monitoring blocks the operation.

The end-to-end acceptance test imports the real SYN snapshot, persists the inherited property contracts, invokes the Cogs, and reads the stored output and statistics back through fresh services and the REST and WebSocket APIs. It also checks that another workspace cannot read those records. Wall time and the controller’s CPU interval are measured; target memory, device usage and costs remain unavailable where they haven’t been observed.

There are shared records for device, profiler and debugger sessions too, including exact target, process and source identities. Registering those records doesn’t establish a working phone connection or hardware probe. Python remains the first separately tested debugger backend. Signed provenance and live discovery have their own later stages.

The code, tests and recorded example are in the Potbot 0.5.0.dev5 source preview and canonical contract guide. This follows the earlier source inventory and Python debugger work.

content.raw:
The next step in Potbot’s tool plan was to check what was already there. Its source contains MCP, command-line and API adapter libraries, along with the debugger added earlier. Those are useful starting points for the remaining work.

I’ve added an inventory that can inspect a committed revision and map its Python modules to the services that own them. It keeps the commit, source and dependency-lock hashes, links the components to the implementation plan, and records its own progress as a SYN Cog.

The first run inspected the existing development-version baseline: 183 Python modules across 16 integration owners. It found source files for MCP stdio and HTTP, command-line tools, HTTP/SDK calls, gRPC, OpenAPI and Python’s debugger protocol. Their presence leaves installation, permissions and execution qualification as separate questions.

In the replay, the Cog starts, records each checked integration owner, and finishes with measured wall time and the controller’s CPU interval. Target CPU, memory and cost remain unavailable where they haven’t been measured. The local demonstration uses labelled test journals; the separate CI acceptance checks durable PostgreSQL storage and the monitoring API.

The owner map is useful when extending the software. Database changes belong in the existing migration system. Credentials stay with the existing security boundary. New execution routes should use the controller, gateway and supervisor already responsible for admission. Finding the right place to extend is part of the implementation work.

An explicitly requested profile still needs its required inputs; it can’t quietly pass by skipping them.

title.raw: Stepping through Python with Potbot
title.rendered: Stepping through Python with Potbot

content.raw:
Potbot can now stop a Python program at a breakpoint, step through its functions and inspect the call stack and local variables. Each operation runs as a SYN Cog, with a record of when it started, what happened while it was running and how it finished.

The interface is language-neutral. Python is the first backend tested, using debugpy. The common operations include launching or attaching to a process, setting breakpoints, stepping over, into and out of functions, inspecting values, and detaching or terminating under the appropriate ownership rules.

The small test program starts with outer(5), calls leaf(10) and returns 33. At the breakpoint, the debugger can see seed=5. Stepping into the next function exposes value=10, while the caller remains visible underneath it. The test checks those actual values and source locations.

In the replay: stop in outer; step over; reject a reference to the previous stack frame; step into leaf; inspect the current function and its caller; step over and out; then continue to an observed exit code of zero. The table shows measured timings from the original Cog calls.

Old stack references matter here. Once a program resumes, a frame from its previous stop may no longer describe the running process. Potbot rejects it rather than quietly inspecting the wrong state. A separate test attaches to an owned Python process, detaches, and verifies that the process is still alive. Another follows an uncaught exception.

The monitoring uses Potbot’s existing execution ledger and artifact storage. Each Cog keeps its typed input, result and binding receipt, together with start, progress and completion events. Wall time and the controller’s CPU interval are measured. Target CPU, memory, GPU use and cost remain explicitly unavailable where there is no qualified measurement; they are not filled in with zeroes.

Testing also found a useful boundary in the sandbox: debugpy needs an internal connection between its adapter and target. Its explicit private-loopback profile now allows that communication inside a separate network namespace. Tests check that host and internet connections remain blocked, along with pathname sockets and filesystem escapes. The default profile still denies sockets.

This is a source preview of the debugger interface, rather than completion of Potbot’s wider tool plan. Other languages, phone control, profiling and remote hardware protocols still need their own adapters and real acceptance tests.

The 0.5.0.dev3 release contains the source and Python package. The debugger guide includes the Cog interface, test commands and recorded example. The Python adapter uses Microsoft’s debugpy and the Debug Adapter Protocol.

title.raw: Giving every object a memory of its own
title.rendered: Giving every object a memory of its own

content.raw:
The direction I want to explore for Potbot and Syn is to give every Syn object a separate memory graph in Potbot. A type, a configured tool, an event and a result would each have a memory of their own.

This is a design proposal from a research review. The separate memory graphs haven’t been implemented or benchmarked.

Remembering what belongs to what

Consider a parser. Its type can describe the contract it should meet. A configured parser can have its own implementation and settings. One attempt to run it is an event, and the result of that attempt is another record.

Keeping those identities separate makes a practical difference. A failed attempt belongs to that attempt’s history. It can teach us something about the configured parser without becoming an inherited fact about every parser of that type.

The graphs could still refer to one another. A question about a tool’s failure could follow a permitted reference to the exact attempt and its result. That reference would need its own access check. Knowing an object exists shouldn’t give an agent access to everything remembered about it.

What the research adds

MAGMA separates several kinds of relationship, including time, entities and inferred causes. Zep’s temporal graph research distinguishes when a fact applied from when the system learnt it. Both ideas would help an object’s memory preserve context as it changes.

MemForest studies how to update hierarchical memory efficiently. Databricks’ MemCurrent research offers another useful comparison: keep the original experience alongside the lessons derived from it.

These approaches address different problems. A summary helps an agent find its way around a long history. A source record lets it check what actually happened. A model’s explanation remains an interpretation, even when it sounds convincing.

A small test before a bigger system

I’d start with a few synthetic objects and give each an empty, separately addressable graph. Then I’d add events, source-linked claims and corrections. One test would use the same object reference in two different source namespaces, to check that their memories stayed separate.

Another would introduce a late correction. The system would need to preserve both what applied at the time and what it knew before the correction arrived. A private result linked from a public object would test whether the boundary held.

Only then would it be useful to compare ordinary search with graph traversal and summaries. The measures would include finding the right evidence, recognising missing information, keeping facts current and the cost of maintaining the memory.

A separate graph for every object needn’t mean a separate database for every object. The storage can be shared while the identities, histories and permissions remain explicit. That is the architecture to test next.

Research checked on 23 October 2026. The linked papers and first-party research reports describe their authors’ methods and results; none establishes that this proposed combination will work well in Potbot. The featured artwork is an original generated concept illustration.

title.raw: Hearing lyric edits while the music plays
title.rendered: Hearing lyric edits while the music plays

content.raw:
Featured artwork: a generated illustration of the article’s subject. Screenshots and demonstrations below show the actual work.

I've added lyric auditioning to React Timeline Sequence. Timed words can now appear as subtitles over the cover artwork while the selected audio channel plays. It makes a timing edit visible in the same place that it will be read.

The subtitles follow the shared transport through play, pause, seeking and loops. Moving a lyric boundary changes the audition immediately, so an editor can check an unsaved adjustment before committing it. Switching audio channels stops the previous source and resets the audition to the new one.

This silent recording shows the real interface using original test artwork, synthetic tones and test lines. It moves between lyric positions, changes a timing, switches the audio channel and exercises a loop. The underlying checks also cover gaps between lines, the end of playback, missing cover artwork and a long line at narrow widths.

The control is released in React Timeline Sequence 0.6.0. Hosts opt in with the lyricAudition option. The integration into StemLab's live and exported viewers has also been merged, and rebuilt local examples have been checked with their saved song data.

That keeps the timing work close to its source. The audio, selected lyric lane and current edit use one transport, rather than leaving a separate subtitle preview to drift away from the edit being tested. The audition guide explains the integration and its limits.

title.raw: What ten music searches showed about KeywordMoves and vidIQ
title.rendered: What ten music searches showed about KeywordMoves and vidIQ

content.raw:
I put KeywordMoves and vidIQ through the same ten music queries, including friendship, grief, protest songs and night driving music. I used vidIQ’s free web interface and KeywordMoves’ Datamuse and Wikipedia adapters, then kept their evidence separate.

vidIQ returned eight numerical seed estimates and two displays below 750. Those are worldwide YouTube estimates. The free KeywordMoves sources returned 226 words or topic titles, without a YouTube search-volume metric. A long candidate list wasn’t answering the same question.

The suggestions needed closer attention too. For “songs about friendship”, vidIQ returned “friendship songs”, “preschool songs” and “songs for kids”. One looked useful for the music I’m researching; the others addressed a different audience.

Across the ten queries, I classified ten of vidIQ’s thirty related suggestions as useful direct listening queries. None of Datamuse’s first three words per query met that criterion. This compares two particular discovery routes, rather than every feature of either tool.

KeywordMoves 0.5.1 now imports saved vidIQ keyword results while preserving country context, censored figures and provider dates. It also adds explicit phrase filters and matching terms, with the original evidence kept alongside every retained candidate.

The filters retained twelve vidIQ suggestions, including all ten I had found useful. They were developed from these same results, so this is an encouraging check on the change, rather than an independent test of how it will perform on new searches.

There’s still a gap: importing vidIQ’s estimates doesn’t give KeywordMoves an independent YouTube demand model. The useful result here is a clearer research queue and a better way to bring sources together, while keeping their limits visible.

Source context: vidIQ keyword research, Datamuse’s word API and the KeywordMoves import and comparison guide.

Further checks on free sources

I extended the source review to 22 services. Some clearly described relative interest, autocomplete suggestions or Google search volumes. Others returned monthly figures that needed more scrutiny. A newly invented random string received 7.2K searches in one tool; another reported 46.6K and then 50.3K on an immediate repeat. I kept those figures out of the demand records. These checks expose a reason to pause, rather than proving how any provider calculates its data.

A useful additional route was vidIQ’s public keyword overview, which showed five US monthly estimates and five rising queries. KeywordMoves 0.5.3 imports reviewed HTML from that feed while retaining rounded displays, source dates and the distinction between monthly counts and seven-day growth. The rising section leaves its geography unstated, so the importer does too.

This expands free access to vidIQ’s data. It still uses the same provider, and the featured feed cannot answer arbitrary keyword queries. The full source audit records the working route, rejected numerical claims and access limits. I haven’t found an additional independent free volume provider that passed these checks.

I also checked sources that offer useful keyword context without a YouTube monthly estimate. KeywordMoves 0.5.4 adds a YT Keyword Tool module for reviewed suggestions and extends Keywords Everywhere with a free import of Google planning figures. The first real replay retained 113 suggestions and 28 rows with Google metrics, keeping batch-relative tiers, Google volumes and paid-ad competition separate. Navid and Keyword Tool Dominator produced many expansions for the invented control string, so their search-data claims remain on hold. Rapidtags required an account and DigestSEO reported an unavailable API key. The module guide explains the working imports and those limits.

Automatic collection, 12 October 2026

KeywordMoves 0.5.5 removes the manual HTML step for the working YT Keyword Tool and Keywords Everywhere routes. It can fetch the first tool’s public-form response directly, or operate the free tools’ ordinary forms through a connected browser and pass the results straight into its existing parsers.

The live check returned 107 suggestions for “songs about friendship”. A bounded Keywords Everywhere harvest displayed 21 rows; 19 contained Google planning figures and two had no measurements to retain. These remain different kinds of evidence: provider-ranked suggestions and Google search context. Neither becomes a measured YouTube monthly total.

The collector checks the visible free quota, keeps the source’s own pacing and stops when access or scope cannot be verified. The public vidIQ HTTP route still returned a rate limit at its robots-policy check, so it stayed unavailable rather than switching clients. No paid calls or new accounts were used. The collection guide explains the direct and browser routes, their limits, and the local handoff needed where a browser host does not permit subprocesses.

Native YouTube Search trends, 13 October 2026

KeywordMoves 0.5.6 adds automatic collection from Google Trends’ normal CSV download. Through a connected browser, it checks the search term, country, date range and YouTube Search filter, downloads the chosen chart and passes the original data straight to the existing parser.

For “songs about friendship”, the live check retained 53 weekly observations and used 52 completed weeks in its summary. A second export contained 31 related-query rows across Top and Rising. These are sampled relative indices and growth displays, including Breakout labels. They don’t supply a YouTube monthly search total.

A connected, authorised browser is still required. The collector stops when access, download or scope checks fail. vidIQ’s public route again returned a rate limit at its robots check, so it remains unavailable. The updated collection guide explains the native download and direct parser handoff. No paid requests or new accounts were used.

Matched comparisons, 13 October 2026

The next sweep returned 1,611 suggestions from 49 generic music topics. The wording still needed a song-fit review: a tutorial, another artist’s track or a children’s song can share words with an original and address the wrong audience. KeywordMoves 0.5.7 can now require both listening context and a relevant topic, while keeping the original source values and reasons for exclusions.

I also compared five terms in one native Google Trends YouTube Search export. That shared comparison matters: five separately scaled peaks of 100 would not tell us which search had more relative interest. The figures below use Worldwide scope and 52 completed weeks from the past-year export; the unfinished week is excluded.

Mean displayed relative index in one shared export, not monthly searches
Search termCompleted-window display
protest songs11.0192
songs about friendship4.6731
night driving music2.8654
songs about griefReporting bounds 0.0961 to below 0.1154
songs about ADHDReporting bounds 0.0192 to below 0.0385

The bounds retain the uncertainty in a displayed “<1”. They are not confidence intervals. The many displayed zeroes for grief and ADHD do not mean nobody searched. Google explains the low-volume threshold and statistical noise; its search-term guide also explains that unquoted terms match their constituent words, rather than only one exact phrase.

These results do not validate or disprove vidIQ’s monthly estimates. The measurement windows, term definitions and sampling differ. Six further free planning collections returned 49 rows with Google figures, which remain Google evidence even though the tool’s page is called a YouTube keyword tool. A longer candidate list still does not give us an independent YouTube volume model.

The native five-term CSV downloaded successfully. A later automated refresh showed a source display error and timed out, so I have not counted it as a successful live multi-term collection. The collector now stops early on that visible error. The assessment guide records the matched-export rules and limits. The released package passed 2,213 Python tests and 37 synthetic browser checks, and its GitHub and PyPI files were verified before installation.

13 October: turning a candidate list into a shortlist

KeywordMoves 0.5.8 adds a reviewed shortlist selector. It works from an exact, hashed candidate pool and recorded judgements about relevance, listening intent and wording. It selects five candidates by default, limits repetition across declared groups, and records selection reasons, omissions and any shortfall.

The selector preserves the source measurements alongside those judgements. It does not infer song fit or produce a new search-volume estimate. A useful phrase still needs a clear connection to the song, and missing YouTube demand remains missing. The shortlist guide explains the review contract and a reproducible example. The release passed 2,243 Python tests and 37 synthetic browser checks; its GitHub and PyPI package files were independently verified before installation.

title.raw: Where my songs have been heard and published so far
title.rendered: Where my songs have been heard and published so far

content.raw:
A few of my songs have now found a place on radio and in published writing. I’ve brought the confirmed publicity together here, with links to the original sources, so there’s a clear record of what has appeared so far.

The articles below are pieces I contributed about the songs and the subjects behind them. The radio entries come from the stations’ own logs. Together, they give several different ways into the music.

Birth Stories: writing, resources and radio

Birth Stories has the widest set of confirmed public appearances so far. Red Devil Radio’s artist log lists 33 plays of the song as checked on 11 October. Its first play was confirmed on 20 August. That is the station’s logged count; I don’t have an audience figure to attach to it.

The writing and resource links are:

  • My account on the Birth Trauma Association’s website, which was public by 4 September and connects the experiences behind the song with the music.
  • Being present is not the same as being included, published by Following Young Fathers Further on 9 September.
  • Listening is part of safety: what three births taught me, published by Sussex Bylines on 8 September and updated on 12 September.
  • The Birth Stories resource entry in the Father Inclusion Hub, linking to the song page and video. The entry was first verified on 10 September; its original publication date isn’t shown.

Dying for a Diagnosis: the waiting list in words

Psychreg published my personal essay, What Does a Waiting List Sound Like?, on 26 August, with an update on 28 August. It connects Dying for a Diagnosis with the research and treatment-access questions behind the song.

Moderate or Good: familiar words in another setting

My Sussex Magazine article, Seaford Artist Finds a New Use for Britain’s Most Familiar Sea-Weather Words, appeared on 20 August. It introduces Moderate or Good and the use it makes of the Shipping Forecast’s language.

Light Will Win: a place on The Local Line-up

V2 Radio’s dated playlist lists Light Will Win (Shubh Diwali) at 21:52 on 7 October, during The Local Line-up. That gives the play a specific date and programme in the station’s public record.

Patriotic Revolution: the cadence behind the song

Dopetrackz has published my article From Livestream Cadence to a 140 BPM Artistic Response, about Patriotic Revolution. The page is dated 8 October, updated on 11 October, and credited to me.

Conversations, and what comes next

Alongside those appearances, I’ve collected my public discussions around Dmitri My Talisman in its discussion journal. Those entries are my own contributions to conversations, rather than reviews or radio plays.

Some upcoming songs are also lined up for further radio play. I’m keeping the details for later, and I’ll add the confirmed plays when they happen.

I’ve added these source links to the relevant song pages too. As more publicity is confirmed, those pages will keep a dated record alongside the music.

title.raw: Bringing more sources into KeywordMoves
title.rendered: Bringing more sources into KeywordMoves

content.raw:
I’ve released KeywordMoves 0.5.0 with more ways to bring useful sources into keyword research. The aim is to give each result enough context to judge what it actually tells us.

A music catalogue can help check a recording’s artist and genre. Article views can show attention around a subject. A keyword provider can estimate searches and competition. Each is useful, but they answer different questions.

Adding catalogue and topic context

The new Apple song reader returns catalogue details such as the track, credited artist and genre. The Wikimedia reader keeps daily article views for a stated date range, including any missing days. Neither turns those records into a claim about demand for a song.

Datamuse also has more context options, including topic hints, neighbouring words and its supported language vocabularies. It helps explore wording; its relevance scores are not search-volume figures.

Keeping the collection deliberate

An explicit research plan can now bring the supported free readers and saved evidence imports together. It keeps the original sources, subjects, dates, scope and units with the results. A failed source remains unavailable rather than quietly becoming a zero.

SE Ranking adds another route for keyword metrics, related phrases and questions. It needs an API key and paid access. The adapter requires a stated credit allowance before a request; that local check is not a guarantee about the provider’s billing. I tested this contract with synthetic responses and haven’t run a paid SE Ranking collection.

What is verified

The free Wikimedia and Apple readers were checked against their live APIs. The release passed 1,994 local tests, with two optional model checks skipped, and all checks on the reviewed pull request passed. GitHub and PyPI package downloads were independently checked against the same checksum manifest.

More sources can improve the questions we ask and the evidence we retain. They don’t prove that every suggested phrase is worthwhile, or that KeywordMoves predicts results better than another tool. Song fit, listener intent and actual search referrals still need their own review.

KeywordMoves 0.5.0 is available on GitHub and PyPI. The multi-source research guide explains the supported routes and their limits. This builds on the earlier evidence-monitoring work.

title.raw: Keeping keyword evidence fresh with KeywordMoves
title.rendered: Keeping keyword evidence fresh with KeywordMoves

content.raw:
I've released KeywordMoves 0.4.0 with a way to keep keyword evidence under review. It now records dated observations, shows gaps in coverage and checks which measurements can sensibly be compared.

The earlier song-keyword review was about finding truthful language for the songs. This update is about keeping the evidence behind that language current.

Keeping different measurements separate

A Google Trends index, a website impression and a YouTube search referral tell me different things. A phrase found in a caption tells me something else again. The monitor keeps the source, metric, date, geography and report scope with each observation.

It can flag a stale report, a failed collection or a missing result. It also keeps the last available observation, so a later failure doesn't quietly become a zero.

Text alternative: the nine-second clip filters the report to Google, then missing coverage, then TikTok, before returning to all rows. The Google example shows a compatible change in website impressions from 10 to 20. The TikTok example has unknown completeness. These invented examples demonstrate the software, not demand for a real song.

A change needs comparable evidence

Change alerts require matching source context and compatible measurements. Rounded estimates, censored values and differently normalised indices don't become precise growth claims. Search Console and channel-performance comparisons also need suitable reporting periods.

The Trends import has been tightened too. Top indices, Rising percentages and Breakout labels keep their own units. A series containing missing or censored points keeps the original points without acquiring an invented exact average.

What still needs checking

The release provides watchlists, history and coverage reporting across the twelve search and social platforms in the review. It can prepare bounded collection plans through the existing Search Console, YouTube Analytics and Bing Webmaster readers.

That doesn't establish account access or a global search-volume figure for every network. Actual permitted exports and authorised account checks are still needed. Installing KeywordMoves doesn't start a background collector or a paid request.

KeywordMoves 0.4.0 is available on GitHub, with installable packages, checksums and a monitoring guide. Its checks passed across Python 3.10–3.13. The next useful step is to verify more real sources and retain their limits alongside their results.

title.raw: Finding the words for a song, without inventing demand
title.rendered: Finding the words for a song, without inventing demand

content.raw:
I’ve been going through the language around my songs: the words in the lyrics, the descriptions on their pages, and the phrases that appear in searches and social-platform discovery tools.

There are two different questions in that work. Does a phrase describe the song honestly? And is there evidence that people search for it? A good answer to the first doesn’t automatically answer the second.

For Moderate or Good, phrases such as “Shipping Forecast song” and “Radio 4 nostalgia song” fit the recording. Those descriptive keywords are now present in its page metadata. That tells me the wording has been implemented. It doesn’t tell me how many people search for it, or whether it will bring anyone to the song.

I’ve also improved KeywordMoves so that a phrase extracted from source text can be traced back to wording that actually appears together. That matters when a tool removes small words and accidentally makes two separated words look like a phrase. The new route preserves literal spans and handles Unicode text, including Persian joining characters.

The review covered 57 songs and 12 agreed search and social platforms, recording usable samples and access gaps separately. Google Trends indices, Search Console exposure, provider estimates and words found in captions measure different things. I haven’t turned them into one popularity score, and a source returning nothing usable stays unavailable rather than becoming zero demand.

The page update is now published. EPK Social Metadata 1.2.0 adds concise descriptive keyword lists and matching Schema.org properties. It also fills 16 missing recording durations where the exact public audio provides the evidence, and supplies missing cover dimensions from the existing upload. Unknown facts remain omitted.

Google doesn’t use HTML meta keywords for indexing or ranking. The clearer descriptions and accurate metadata are useful housekeeping; I haven’t measured a ranking benefit from these changes.

The next useful step is better demand evidence: first-party search queries, the actual search terms that lead people to videos, and properly scoped related or rising trends. I’ll need a settled period after the changes before comparing outcomes. More words in a database won’t answer that question on their own.

title.raw: Codex helped me make a political song. Then it refused to promote the cause.
title.rendered: Codex helped me make a political song. Then it refused to promote the cause.

content.raw:
I’ve spent much of today working with Codex on my new song, Free Danny Tommo.

It helped me check the master, compare lyric timings, analyse the track, build visual ideas, create three promotional Shorts, improve the press page and research places where the song might find an audience. It was prepared to do a remarkable amount of work around a political record.

Then I asked it to help promote the cause behind the song, and it drew a line.

That is the part I find difficult to accept. The system can help me make the megaphone. It can inspect the words coming through it. It can design the poster, time the captions and research the audience. When I ask it to help carry the political message to that audience, it suddenly becomes cautious about political advocacy.

In my view, Codex has been politically neutered.

I understand why a company building a general-purpose AI system would be nervous about political influence. I don’t want a machine secretly deciding elections or impersonating people. That is a very different thing from helping an independent artist promote his own clearly attributed political song.

I am not asking Codex to invent a belief for me. The belief, the song and the decision to publish it are mine. I am asking the tool to help with the same practical work it would apparently perform for a song about almost any less contentious subject: finding relevant outlets, preparing accurate material and getting it in front of people who may want to hear it.

There is something strange about a tool being capable enough to participate in nearly every stage of a political artwork, while being deliberately limited at the point where that artwork might actually influence anyone.

To be fair, Codex did not abandon the project. It completed extensive audience-neutral research, built a year-long marketing plan and helped keep the factual claims and evidence in order. It also helped me finish the public Free Danny Tommo press page. The limitation appeared when promotion crossed from marketing a piece of music into advancing the political cause expressed by it.

That distinction may make sense inside a policy document. From an artist’s side of the screen, it feels artificial. Political art is made to communicate a political point. Removing the final act of communication does not make the earlier work neutral.

I will carry on promoting the song myself. I will also probably look for, or build, an alternative that treats me as responsible for my own political voice instead of trying to remove politics from the tool at the moment it matters.

That does not mean I want an AI to tell me what to believe. I want tools that help me express what I already believe, openly and in my own name.

The song is available through the official press page, Spotify and YouTube.

title.raw: Putting section cues on the beat with StemLab and DanceMoves
title.rendered: Putting section cues on the beat with StemLab and DanceMoves

content.raw:
I’ve extended StemLab’s timing workflow so that full-track analysis can produce section cues for DanceMoves, with one important rule: a cue only moves onto a detected beat when the beat is genuinely nearby.

That sounds like a small detail, but it makes a real difference. A section marker can be structurally sensible and still land a fraction before or after the musical pulse. When that marker drives an EPK effect, the visual response feels slightly detached from the track.

For cue sheets that already existed, the new matcher checks the surrounding beat evidence and allows a maximum adjustment of 150 milliseconds. It never forces a distant match. Openings at zero stay at zero when there is no suitable nearby beat, and every machine-assisted change remains visible in the review report.

For forthcoming releases without cue sheets, StemLab now takes the longer route: source separation, speech and lyric evidence where available, functional section analysis, and several independent beat detectors. The generated LRC keeps the model’s section labels and records which boundaries were already exact, which were snapped, and which still need review.

Beat This was the missing part of that detector set. The code was present, but its official checkpoint was not available locally. I repaired the dependency path, pinned the official model file in StemLab’s project cache, verified its hash, and ran it against a real track before using it in the catalogue pass.

The full profile also exposed a useful hardware boundary. One optional separator, MVSep Mega53, documents a 16 GB VRAM requirement, while the current project GPU has about 8 GB. StemLab now records that model as unavailable before inference instead of provoking a predictable crash, then continues with the other eligible backends. That is more honest than quietly dropping the model or pretending the result exists.

The WordPress side is deliberately simple. Each release page already has an EPK Timing panel for BPM, lyric timing, cue timing and its chosen ambient effect. The new cue file is selected there without changing the page’s BPM. DanceMoves can then use the file on that release only, while its repeating musical effects remain confined to their declared visual subjects rather than flashing or tinting the whole page.

The catalogue pass covers 17 upcoming EPKs: four existing cue sheets were aligned conservatively and thirteen releases received new provisional cue sets from full analysis. All 17 cue settings now persist in WordPress, and every rendered EPK reports the exact selected cue file with its timing catalogue ready. Existing BPM properties were left alone throughout, including pages that deliberately use DanceMoves’ labelled fallback.

These are still analysis-assisted boundaries, not a substitute for listening. The useful change is that the machine work is now reproducible, reviewable and connected to the page that will actually use it.

title.raw: Giving song links a better chance of a playable preview
title.rendered: Giving song links a better chance of a playable preview

content.raw:
I’ve updated the metadata behind my song pages so a link can point to a public video as well as the artwork and audio. The aim is to make it easier to start listening when a search or sharing service supports a playable preview.

The update covers 35 public YouTube recordings and the landscape visualiser for Light Will Win. Some of the YouTube recordings are Art Tracks or official audio uploads, so their descriptions reflect what they actually show. Pages without a verified video keep their existing artwork and audio metadata.

The video’s title, thumbnail, publication date and duration are stored separately from the song’s release details. Google’s embedded-video markup is added only when that exact video is embedded in the EPK and the required facts are known. A link alone doesn’t qualify. The first-publication date of the Light Will Win video is still unconfirmed, so it’s left blank.

All 35 YouTube players started after one click in the deployed player, and the native Light Will Win video plays too. Checks across all 54 EPKs confirmed that their existing page bodies, artwork and audio references were preserved. Google’s Rich Results Test detected one valid video item on the Amnesty EPK.

That’s useful validation, but it isn’t a promise of a play button wherever a link appears. Google generally reserves video results for pages centred on watching a video, and sharing services decide how they display a card. The new fields give them accurate information to work with.

The plugin is available as Kieran EPK Social Metadata 1.1.0.

title.raw: Connecting the parts of DanceFlow
title.rendered: Connecting the parts of DanceFlow

content.raw:
I've been building several tools around the same practical problem: how to make visual work respond to music deliberately, without pretending one model or one application knows everything.

Those tools now have a clearer shared name and shape. DanceFlow is the route between them.

Three different jobs

StemLab looks at the music. It brings tempo, beats, structure, stems, harmony, lyric timing and other evidence onto a shared clock.

DanceRudiments describes movement in musical time. Its job is not to analyse the song or draw a finished page. It provides deterministic position functions that another application can sample and scale.

DanceMoves brings timed effects into the browser and WordPress. It schedules BPM, cue and lyric responses while keeping reduced-motion, keyboard use and performance fallbacks in view.

They can work together, but they don't need to be installed together. That boundary matters. An analysis result is not a movement, and a movement function is not proof that a public page works.

The work around the motion

DanceFlow also includes tools around that core path. KeywordMoves keeps search and language evidence in its original units and scopes. RasterMoves prepares and enlarges imagery while recording model and processing provenance. PixelCue helps inspect and tag visual-media collections locally.

The common idea is not that every task needs a large platform. It is that useful evidence should stay inspectable as it moves from one stage to the next.

A public home for it

I've put together a standalone DanceFlow page with the core path, the supporting tools and links to source and demonstrations. It sits alongside the other projects on this site rather than inside My Songs, because it is software rather than a release.

There is a downloadable DanceRudiments visualiser if you want to try the movement side without setting up a project, and the Arcadians press page is one public example of DanceMoves responding to a track's structure and pulse.
