title.raw: Releasing ThumbMoves: a small Python library for thumbnail caches
title.rendered: Releasing ThumbMoves: a small Python library for thumbnail caches

content.raw:
PixelCue needs small preview images, but opening and decoding every original file just to draw a thumbnail is wasteful. Desktop operating systems often already have the right image in their thumbnail cache. ThumbMoves is the small library I have separated out to ask for that cached image without quietly doing the expensive fallback itself.

Version 0.1.0 is now available on PyPI. It has one deliberately conservative contract: return a cached thumbnail when the operating system already has one, or return a miss. It does not open the source media file and it does not trigger thumbnail generation.

One boundary instead of three copies

On Windows, ThumbMoves uses the Shell thumbnail interface with cache-only and thumbnail-only flags. On Linux and other Freedesktop-style desktops, it looks up the standard thumbnail-cache path derived from the file URI. macOS does not expose an equivalent public, strict cache-only lookup, so the current backend returns a miss rather than pretending it can keep the same promise.

That last detail is important. A cross-platform API is only useful if the shared name does not hide materially different behaviour. PixelCue can try ThumbMoves first and decide what to do after a miss, while another application can make a different choice.

Separating the code also gives it a proper reusable boundary. PixelCue no longer needs to own a one-off copy of the cache logic, and other Python tools can install the same small package.

A release route that can be repeated

The package now has cross-platform GitHub Actions checks, wheel and source-archive validation, and a tag-driven release workflow. Production publication uses PyPI's trusted-publishing route, so the workflow exchanges its GitHub identity for a short-lived publishing token rather than storing a permanent PyPI password in the repository.

The release job also creates a matching GitHub Release with the wheel, source archive and a SHA256SUMS.txt file. I checked the public PyPI files against those GitHub assets, then installed version 0.1.0 into a clean Python 3.13 environment and ran the installed command-line help.

TestPyPI is not part of this first completed route. I deliberately left that optional path aside for now rather than holding up the production package.

Where it is now

ThumbMoves 0.1.0 supports Python 3.10 and later and is released under the MIT licence. The package is available from PyPI, with the matching files and checksums on the GitHub release.

It is a small piece of PixelCue, but that is rather the point: one narrow job, an honest platform contract and a release process that can be repeated without turning the library back into a private implementation detail.

title.raw: RasterMoves: making every image run improve the next one
title.rendered: RasterMoves: making every image run improve the next one

content.raw:
RasterMoves is the image-upscaling part of my DanceFlow work. It runs locally and uses model manifests from OpenModelDB, with support for PyTorch, ONNX and optional generative refinement.

The immediate job is to make an image larger. The more useful long-term job is to notice what made that run awkward, uncertain or repetitive, then make the tool a little better before the next image arrives. I have now added a reusable skill that makes that feedback loop explicit.

A run should leave the tool better

The workflow has six stages: run RasterMoves deliberately, verify the output and its provenance, capture any friction, make the smallest reusable fix, document it with a real example, then commit and verify the change on GitHub.

That final step matters. A local edit is not the same thing as a published improvement, so the workflow checks the remote commit as well as the code and documentation. If a screenshot genuinely explains the change, it belongs in the README too; if it adds no useful evidence, it does not.

The new skill lives with the repository rather than in one particular machine setup. It includes an evaluation checklist, example prompts and a Potential problems section for fixes that should not have to be rediscovered.

A complete local setup

I also built a clean Python 3.13 environment containing every compatible optional RasterMoves feature group:

  • CUDA-enabled PyTorch and torchvision
  • ONNX Runtime GPU support
  • generative refinement and tracing support
  • Google Drive downloads
  • extra Spandrel architectures
  • the full development and test toolchain

The CPU-only ONNX package is intentionally absent because the project documentation warns against installing it alongside the GPU build.

What the checks prove

RasterMoves' diagnostic command sees the NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti through PyTorch CUDA, and ONNX Runtime reports TensorRT, CUDA and CPU providers. The environment's 67 installed packages pass their compatibility check.

The full automated suite completed with 347 passing tests and 5 skips. The skipped cases are opt-in tests that require downloading pretrained model weights, so this result verifies the software environment rather than claiming a visual-quality result. No pretrained weights were downloaded for this setup, and no image-quality comparison was made.

That distinction is useful with image upscaling. A neural model can reconstruct plausible texture, and generative refinement can synthesise detail; neither should be described as recovering forensic truth from the source image.

Ready for the next image

The repository now documents both the complete installation and the improvement loop. The aim is simple: each real image gives RasterMoves another chance to become clearer, safer and easier to use.

The source, installation instructions and workflow are available in the RasterMoves repository.

title.raw: Teaching KeywordMoves to see with PixelCue
title.rendered: Teaching KeywordMoves to see with PixelCue

content.raw:
I’ve been joining two of my local tools together. PixelCue can look at images and other visual media; KeywordMoves keeps keyword evidence from different sources separate instead of flattening everything into one pretend score. The missing piece was a clean way for one to ask the other a very small question: what keywords do you see in this file?

PixelCue now has a simple local REST service. A client sends one file path to /v1/keywords and gets a plain JSON list back. KeywordMoves has a matching pixelcue operation and a keyword-only output mode, so the smallest useful run really does return only the phrases.

The server is also the foundation for PixelCue’s planned React interface. The current Python desktop interface is useful while the analysis code develops, but the longer-term shape is a local web service with more than one possible client. Keeping analysis behind a documented endpoint means the web interface, KeywordMoves and future tools do not all need their own copies of the model-loading logic.

Making slow downloads visible

The slightly awkward part is the first model run. Hugging Face can take bloody ages to download model weights, and an ordinary HTTP request can look dead even when useful work is still happening.

PixelCue therefore exposes request-scoped Socket.IO updates alongside the REST endpoint. A client can subscribe using the request ID and see inspection, model loading, model-download, analysis, completion and failure stages. KeywordMoves allows six hours by default for this particular operation. That is deliberately generous; it avoids turning a slow first download into a false timeout and another unnecessary attempt.

Progress is still only progress. The final REST response or failure remains the actual result.

Keeping the evidence honest

The integration treats PixelCue’s output as visual semantic evidence. If a model returns phrases such as a place, object, colour or mood, those can become candidates to research. They do not prove that anybody searches for the phrase, that it will rank, or that the same phrase is popular on a social platform.

That separation matters to KeywordMoves. Search Console impressions, Google Trends indices, platform-native observations and model-generated visual tags answer different questions. The new plugin records which model and endpoint produced the tags instead of making them look like universal keyword scores.

What I verified

The focused PixelCue service tests passed, as did live health and WebSocket checks. The complete KeywordMoves suite passed 1,809 tests with two skips. I also forced a real Socket.IO client to use WebSocket transport, subscribed it to a request room and checked the acknowledgement.

The React interface is still to come, and I have not treated this work as a finished public release. What is now in place is the reusable seam underneath it: one-file visual keyword extraction over REST, with enough live progress to make the slow first model download understandable rather than mysterious.

title.raw: A small CSS rule made the Arcadians arcade work harder than it should
title.rendered: A small CSS rule made the Arcadians arcade work harder than it should

content.raw:
The Arcadians press page has a little arcade playing behind the artwork. Ships weave between stone tablets and fire in time with the song. It has a frame-rate fallback intended to keep that scene manageable on slower screens by reducing the number of moving pieces.

That fallback had a surprisingly small flaw. It marked spare ships as hidden, but the page's own CSS still told the browser to display them. Another rule, meant to hide extra tablets at the lowest setting, counted the ship images first and hid all the tablets. So the game could look as if it had reset while the browser still painted ships it was meant to remove.

I've fixed both rules. In a controlled slowdown of the live page, the lowest setting now showed two ships and six tablets, with none of the hidden pieces still painted. On a fresh normal load, the full group was still there. The collision shapes also sit closer to the visible ships and tablets, with a narrow contact area for bullets, so near misses are less likely to become explosions. Firing is still tied to the song's 145 BPM pulse.

That fixed the fallback, but not the gradual slowdown I could still see. A second issue was in DanceMoves, the shared timing code behind the press pages. Each time the ships moved, it rescanned the page and added another copy of its generated CSS. In one long-running test that stylesheet grew to more than 1.3 million characters, even though the number of ships and tablets had dropped.

I've updated DanceMoves so ordinary movement doesn't trigger that scan, and a genuine rescan replaces its generated rules instead of piling them up. Version 3.1.7 is now live. In a fresh public Arcadians test, the stylesheet stayed at 885 characters after more than two minutes while all eight ships and 28 tablets remained in play. The release tests and publication workflow passed too.

That is a measured fix for the growing stylesheet, not a guarantee of smooth playback on every device. I still want to check a lower-powered machine for longer. Chips and Ketchup uses the same shared code, but its song-driven visuals still slow down in Brave; that needs its own playback diagnosis rather than assuming this change solved it.

title.raw: Introducing StemLab: a closer look inside a song
title.rendered: Introducing StemLab: a closer look inside a song

content.raw:
Recently I've been building StemLab, a local music-analysis toolkit for getting a clearer picture of what is happening inside a song.

It grew out of a practical problem. I wanted better evidence for timing visual effects and choosing sections for Shorts, without relying on one BPM estimate or treating the output of a single model as the answer. A song can be rhythmically steady but shift phase, a section label can be plausible but wrong, and a cut that looks neat on a timeline can still click or clip a vocal when it repeats.

StemLab brings several kinds of evidence together on the same clock. Depending on the selected analysis profile, it can produce separated stems, beat and downbeat grids, tempo-regime analysis, song structure, harmony, key and tuning evidence, melody and note data, loudness and dynamics, timbre, stereo information, speech and lyric timing, and semantic summaries.

It also finds candidate loops for verses and choruses. These are aligned to complete bars and retain exact source-sample boundaries. StemLab checks the beat grid, available vocal evidence and the waveform on every channel around the join. If a section does not have enough trustworthy evidence, it is left unresolved rather than being forced into a confident-looking result. Listening is still part of the final check.

Keeping the evidence inspectable

The most important part for me is not simply producing a large folder of model output. StemLab records the source hash, the tools and settings used, backend errors and hashes for its generated artefacts. Numerical results are available in JSON, TSV and NPZ files, and it can create a portable Sonic Visualiser session.

There is also a browser workspace built around the separate react-timeline-sequence control. It places playback, waveforms, spectrograms, beats, sections, lyrics and loop candidates under one shared playhead, so the relationships are easier to inspect instead of being scattered across unrelated reports.

Where it fits

StemLab is the music-understanding part of my wider DanceFlow work. Its timing and analysis artefacts can feed motion-aware projects such as the WordPress DanceMoves plugin, but StemLab is not tied to WordPress and is useful on its own.

It can be used as a command-line tool, Python library, local web service, container or local Codex MCP plugin. The public Python distribution is called danceflow-stemlab because package-registry names are globally unique; the project, Python import and command are all still called StemLab.

The full analysis can be deliberately demanding, particularly when the large separation models are enabled, so there is a lighter practical profile for iteration. Optional models also retain their own licences and runtime requirements. StemLab's source is MIT licensed, but that does not silently change the terms attached to third-party model weights.

Getting BeatNet working on current Python

One practical snag was BeatNet. Its current PyPI release pins an old combination of Numba and NumPy that cannot be resolved alongside the maintained madmom-prebuilt package. The model code itself still works on current Python once that old package metadata is kept separate from the runtime.

In my current development checkout, StemLab now treats BeatNet as a pinned external runtime. It downloads the official BeatNet 1.1.3 wheel, checks the SHA-256 published by PyPI, and exposes only the code and bundled weights from its cache. Offline DBN decoding uses madmom-prebuilt. If the runtime is missing or the hash is wrong, StemLab reports it as unavailable rather than pretending that detector ran.

I tested the real model on CPython 3.13.14 with a deterministic 16-second click track at 120 BPM. BeatNet returned 120.0 BPM, 32 beats and 16 downbeats, and StemLab wrote both its JSON and TSV results. That proves the installation, inference and output path; it does not prove that BeatNet will be right about every song.

This is still worth fixing upstream. BeatNet's open installation issue records the released Numba-pin problem, while the current source has already relaxed the worst of those old pins. A focused pull request could finish the job by using a modern offline decoder dependency, keeping PyAudio optional, and testing Python 3.11 to 3.13 before a fresh release. Until that happens, StemLab's verified bootstrap keeps the workaround narrow and reproducible.

What changed in StemLab 1.2

StemLab 1.2 adds several ways of getting more specific evidence without rerunning the whole analysis. It can now compare an LRC cue sheet with an existing beat grid and produce a separate review copy. Nearby timestamps can be snapped precisely, while distant or forced changes stay flagged rather than quietly becoming the new truth.

There is also a new audio-to-MIDI layer. It includes Basic Pitch for isolated pitched parts, specialist piano routes, and multi-instrument options. Each model keeps its own MIDI and normalised note data, but the result is still an inference from audio. A model's tempo events do not replace StemLab's measured beat grid.

A separate evidence layer can add vocal-activity, forced lyric-alignment, pitch, song-structure, harmony and drum hypotheses. The useful part is that these results stay independent: they can support or challenge another result without rewriting approved lyrics, section names or timing. Some research models need their own Python environment or separately licensed weights, so StemLab lists what is available without pretending that every model is ready to run.

StemLab 1.2.0 is now available from the GitHub repository. The README contains the installation options, analysis detail, examples and current limitations. You can also browse the rest of my music work in My Songs.

A focused pull request could finish the job by using a modern offline decoder dependency, keeping PyAudio optional, and testing Python 3.11 to 3.13 before a fresh release. Until that happens, StemLab’s verified bootstrap keeps the workaround narrow and reproducible.

What changed in StemLab 1.2

StemLab 1.2 adds several ways of getting more specific evidence without rerunning the whole analysis. It can now compare an LRC cue sheet with an existing beat grid and produce a separate review copy. Nearby timestamps can be snapped precisely, while distant or forced changes stay flagged rather than quietly becoming the new truth.

There is also a new audio-to-MIDI layer. It includes Basic Pitch for isolated pitched parts, specialist piano routes, and multi-instrument options. Each model keeps its own MIDI and normalised note data, but the result is still an inference from audio. A model’s tempo events do not replace StemLab’s measured beat grid.

A separate evidence layer can add vocal-activity, forced lyric-alignment, pitch, song-structure, harmony and drum hypotheses. The useful part is that these results stay independent: they can support or challenge another result without rewriting approved lyrics, section names or timing. Some research models need their own Python environment or separately licensed weights, so StemLab lists what is available without pretending that every model is ready to run.

StemLab 1.2.0 is now available from the GitHub repository. The README contains the installation options, analysis detail, examples and current limitations. You can also browse the rest of my music work in My Songs.

I used to maintain a blog and write in it once a week (old blog entries now lost), and I wish I still had time and motivation to do that, as I do feel it's a helpful process to go though, to clarify your own thoughts, and also get feedback on them. I will try to pick this habit back up again, but it definitely won't be every week.
